title: 7  Friction
text:
7.1 Basic Theory
Many school physics courses teach friction in a way that inadvertently fosters confusion. In one lesson, students are told to “ignore air resistance” when solving problems about falling objects or moving cars, treating the world as if friction only exists between solid surfaces. Yet in the very next lesson, they’re taught about parachutists whose survival depends entirely on air resistance, suddenly elevating it from negligible to crucial. This abrupt switch can make friction—and forces in general—seem like arbitrary, context-dependent rules rather than consistent physical principles. Instead of helping students see friction as a family of forces (including air resistance) that always oppose motion, we often isolate topics in a fragmented way, leaving learners unsure when and why certain forces matter…

title: 7  Friction
text:
7.1.1 What is Friction?

Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact.
It acts parallel to the surfaces and opposite to the direction of motion or impending motion.



7.1.2 Types of Friction

Static Friction (\(F_s\)): Acts when surfaces are not moving relative to each other. It prevents motion.
Kinetic (Sliding) Friction (\(F_k\)): Acts when surfaces slide past each other.
Rolling Friction: Opposes motion when an object rolls over a surface (usually smaller than sliding friction).



7.1.3 Coefficient of Friction

A dimensionless number representing the frictional properties of surfaces.
Denoted by:

\(\mu_s\) for static friction
\(\mu_k\) for kinetic friction




7.1.4 Frictional Force Formula

Maximum static friction force before motion starts: \[
F_s \leq \mu_s N
\]
Kinetic friction force during sliding: \[
F_k = \mu_k N
\] Where:
\(N\) = normal force (perpendicular force between surfaces)



7.1.5 Characteristics of Friction

Friction depends on:

Nature of surfaces in contact (material, roughness)
Normal force \(N\)

Friction is independent of contact area for solid surfaces.
Friction converts kinetic energy into heat.



7.1.6 Effects of Friction

Enables walking, driving, and gripping.
Causes wear and tear.
Causes energy loss in machines.



7.1.7 Overcoming Friction

Lubrication reduces friction by adding a thin layer between surfaces.
Using rollers or ball bearings reduces friction by converting sliding to rolling friction.



7.1.8 Example: Force Required to Move an Object
If an object of weight \(W\) rests on a horizontal surface:

Normal force \(N = W = mg\)
Minimum force \(F\) to overcome static friction: \[
F = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg
\]

title: 7  Friction
text:
7.2 Stories to enrich

7.2.1 The Tragedy on the Rails: The Tay Bridge Disaster (1879)





One stormy night in Scotland, a passenger train attempted to cross the Tay Bridge. A violent gust struck, and the bridge collapsed beneath it. Investigators later found that oscillations and lack of lateral frictional damping in the bridge design had allowed the wind to amplify motion until the structure gave way. The disaster shocked Victorian engineers. The need to understand not just force, but friction and resistance within joints and tracks, became a central lesson in civil engineering.


7.2.2 The Match That Changed the World





In 1826, John Walker invented the friction match—by accident. Stirring a mixture of chemicals with a stick, he noticed the dry blob at the end flared when scraped on stone. This wasn’t heat from fire—it was the mechanical friction of scraping. The invention allowed for easy fire-making for the first time in history. Friction, normally a nuisance to be avoided, became a tool for ignition and survival.


7.2.3 The Ice of the Battle of Stalingrad





During WWII, German tanks bogged down outside Stalingrad, partly because of brutal cold. The steel tank treads, designed for European mud, couldn’t grip the icy roads. Soviet engineers had reinforced their own equipment with roughened track pads and sandbags for added grip. The frictionless Russian winter became a weapon, turning mobility into paralysis.


7.2.4 Da Vinci’s Secret Notes on Friction

Long before Newton, Leonardo da Vinci discovered fundamental laws of friction while sketching machines. He wrote (in mirrored script!) that the force of friction is proportional to the load and independent of contact area—ideas later attributed to Amontons. He even created diagrams of inclined planes and sliding blocks. But his findings weren’t published for centuries.
Reflection: How might physics history have changed if da Vinci’s friction laws had been shared?


7.2.5 The Ancient Egyptian Sled and the Water Trick

Wall paintings show Egyptians hauling giant statues on sleds. Archaeologists puzzled over how they moved such loads. Then, a modern experiment revealed: adding small amounts of water to the sand increased friction’s efficiency by reducing sand displacement and increasing cohesion—making the sled slide more easily. They weren’t just brute-forcing it. They had mastered frictional control. A painting from the tomb of Djehutihotep also depicts someone pouring liquid in front of a sled, supporting this theory. 
Reflection: How can more friction sometimes make things slide more easily?


7.2.6 The Ice That Was Too Smooth
A group of Gentoo penguins at an aquarium in Hull had to be temporarily removed from their exhibit because new fake ice flooring proved too slippery. 
Staff at The Deep have since installed special anti-slip covering for the seven resident penguins.A staff member said:

The penguins were taken out of the display on January 6 (2014) to do some routine maintenance work but, when we put them back, the covering did not have enough grip in it for them to stick on to and we had a bit of a skidding situation.



7.2.7 The Mystery of the Climbing Gecko





Geckos can walk across ceilings, and for years no one knew how. It wasn’t suction or glue—it was molecular friction. Tiny hairs on their feet use van der Waals forces to generate friction at the atomic scale. Engineers now study geckos to make biomimetic pads that let robots and humans stick to glass walls.


7.2.8 The Violinist’s Rosin
String players rub rosin onto their bows—not to reduce friction, but to create just the right amount. The bow must grip and release the string rapidly to make it vibrate. Too little friction, and there’s no sound. Too much, and it scratches. Musicians become masters of microscopic friction control.

title: 7  Friction
text:
7.3 Practical work and Demos

7.3.1 Ball falling in a tube
Not the most exciting titoe but a great demo. Set up a vertical tube and drop a ping-pong ball into it. The diameter of the tube should be just a little larger than the diameter of the ball. As close as possible is most effective. The ball falls really slowly due to air friction in the tube and quickly reaches terminal velocity.

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Large diameter glass tube up to two metres long •Polystyrene balls of various diameters up to almost that of the internal diameter of the glass tube •Stop clock •Ruler



7.3.2 Glass syringe air bearing
A gas syringe can act like an air bearing when its plunger is fixed and the outer barrel is rotated. By trapping a thin layer of air between the plunger and the barrel wall, the syringe creates a cushion that reduces friction, allowing the barrel to spin smoothly around the stationary plunger. This effect mimics an air bearing’s principle, where pressurized air supports and separates moving parts, enabling low-friction, low-wear rotation. Such a setup can be a useful classroom demonstration of how air bearings work in precision engineering and machinery.


7.3.3 Lowering friction with magnets
Take a magnet and mount it in a clamp with the poles vertically above each other. Take several clean ball bearings and attach them to the magnet so that they hang in a line from the lower end. Hang enough such that a large washer or other steel disc of about 3 cm in diameter only just able to hang from the end. The disc is supported with minimal friction and by blowing on the side of the disc to set it rotating the disc can be set spinning. With some care in the setup, the disc will spin for over 10 minutes.

Age range: 11-13
Apparatus required: •Retort stand and clamp •Two or three ball bearings (diameter about 0.8 mm depending on magnet strength) •Strong bar magnet •Steel disc



7.3.4 Spinning Eggs
Setup: Spin a hardboiled egg and a raw egg horizontally on a table. Touch each to stop it, then release.
Observation: The hardboiled egg stops; the raw egg restarts spinning due to the fluid inside continuing to rotate and dragging on the inside of the shell.


7.3.5 Stick-slip motion
The stick-slip motion in friction is beautifully illustrated by the sliding woodpecker. This is a small wooden bird fixed to a bead by a short spring. The bead fits loosely over a vertical metal rod. When the bird is still it does not slide down but as soon as it is twanged it slips jerkily down the rod.

Theory/Explanation:
The hole in the wooden bead is slightly bigger than the diameter of the metal rod. When the hole is vertical the bead slips down but as soon as it tilts, the bead “grips” the rod. The oscillatory motion of the bird on the spring alternately puts the hole upright and at an angle.
Age range: 11-14
Apparatus required: •Woodpecker toy (available from toy suppliers in England)



7.3.6 Two simple hovercraft
(a) Balloon hovercraft
Drill a hole through the centre of a circular disc of hardboard (disc diameter about 10 cm). Stick a rubber bung over the centre of the disc so that the hole in the bung coincides with the hole in the disc. Blow up a balloon and then fit it over the open end of the bung. Air rushes through the hole, and out the other side of the disc and this acts like a small hovercraft. (b) Tile hovercraft
A simple hovercraft can be made really cheaply by using a computer-cooling fan fixed above a hole in a ceiling tile.

Age range: 11-13
Apparatus required: •Balloon •Hardboard disc with a hole and tube •Ceiling tile •Computer cooling fan



7.3.7 Falling matchbox
This fascinating short experiment shows you how energy is absorbed by friction. Take a match box—a big one is more impressive and you can leave the matches in it.
Making sure that the box is closed (Photo 1), drop in on to a hard surface from a height of about 10cm. The matchbox will bounce and fall over.
Now pull the drawer out slightly (Photo 2) and repeat the experiment. Once again the matchbox hits the table, but this time the drawer slides in a bit, absorbing some of the energy, and the matchbox should stay upright rather than bouncing.
Age range: 14-18 1 2

Apparatus required: ’Hard surface
•Matchbox full of matches



7.3.8 Rolling cans of dog food and baked beans
Get two cans of equal mass — one containing dog food (or cat food for cat lovers) and the other containing baked beans.
Hold them side-by-side at the top of a ramp and then let them go at the same time asking the class which one will reach the bottom of the slope first.
The can of dog food gets there first because the baked beans are moving within the other can, creating frictional forces which slow down the rate of rotation of that can and so making it roll slower.
Then try two cans of fizzy drink but shake one first. See which one wins in this case.

Age range: 11-18 depending on treatment
Apparatus required: •Wooden ramp about 1.5 m long •Tins of dog food, baked beans and two of fizzy drink



7.3.9 Friction between books
A very simple and yet impressive example of friction can be seen using two paper-backed books. It is best done with ones made from rougher poor quality paper.
Hold the books with their open sides facing each other and carefully interleave the pages so that about half of one book extends into half the other as shown by the diagram.
Then get two people to hold the books by their spines and try and pull them apart. There is so much friction between the pages that it is likely that the books will be damaged before they can be pulled apart — so be careful!

Age range: 5-14
Apparatus required: •Two paper-backed books

Lifting a 1kg Mass with Rope on a Cylinder
Setup: Tie a 1kg mass (or tin of beans) to thick string. Wrap the string a few times around a rolling pin (or wine bottle).
Question: What happens when the rod is lifted?
Answer: A few turns of rope hold the mass without slipping - this leads onto the next one beautifully…

The Falling Cup

Setup: About 1m of string is placed over a pencil with a china cup at one end, close to the pencil. The other longer end is tied to a cork. The string is held just below horizontal.
Question: Will the cup reach the ground when released?
Answer: It stops before it reaches the ground, if the string is measured just right. Conservation of inertia causes the cork to increase in angular velocity as the string shortens. The increased velocity causes the cork to wrap the string round the pencil and thereby provide the friction to slow and stop the cup’s descent.

Coin and Paper Drop

Drop separately, then drop with paper side-on and next to coin, finally drop with coin on top of paper, but close.
Observations:
Coin lands first - it has a higher terminal velocity.
Both land together, if paper continues to fall edge-on.
Coin first, paper slips off.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.1 Introduction
phyphox (pronounced “fee-focks”) stands for Physical Phone Experiments. It is a free mobile app designed to transform your smartphone into a powerful physics laboratory. Developed by researchers at RWTH Aachen University in Germany, phyphox leverages the multitude of sensors embedded in modern smartphones—such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, barometers, microphones, and cameras—to perform real-time physics experiments.
Since its launch, phyphox has become an invaluable tool for educators, students, and enthusiasts around the world, enabling hands-on learning that is accessible, versatile, and engaging.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.2 Why phyphox?
Smartphones are ubiquitous, and their built-in sensors are sophisticated enough to measure physical phenomena with surprising accuracy. phyphox harnesses these capabilities by providing easy-to-use experimental setups that require minimal additional equipment. This democratizes physics experimentation by removing traditional barriers like expensive lab gear or dedicated sensors.
Key advantages include:

Accessibility: Available for free on both Android and iOS.
Portability: Experiments can be done anywhere—classrooms, outdoors, or at home.
Interactivity: Real-time data visualization and analysis within the app.
Flexibility: Customizable experiments and exportable raw data for further study.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.3 Core Features

1.3.1 1. Sensor-Based Experiments
phyphox offers dozens of predefined experiments using smartphone sensors, including:

Accelerometer: Measure acceleration, free fall, pendulum motion, or vibrations.
Gyroscope: Analyze rotational motion and angular velocity.
Magnetometer: Detect magnetic fields, measure Earth’s magnetic flux density.
Barometer: Investigate pressure changes, altitude, and weather-related phenomena.
Microphone: Study sound waves, frequency analysis, and resonance.
Light Sensor & Camera: Explore optics, light intensity, and color analysis.
Proximity Sensor: Time-of-flight measurements and simple motion detection.



1.3.2 2. Real-Time Data Display and Processing

Live graphs and numerical data display.
Basic data analysis functions like integration, differentiation, and Fourier transform.
Adjustable sampling rates and data smoothing.
Customizable experiment parameters.



1.3.3 3. Data Export and Sharing
phyphox allows exporting data in standard formats such as CSV, facilitating deeper analysis using spreadsheet software or scientific tools like Python, MATLAB, or Excel.


1.3.4 4. Custom Experiments
Users with technical skills can create or modify experiments using the phyphox experiment file format—a simple XML-based configuration that defines sensors, data processing, and user interface elements. This flexibility supports educators and researchers in tailoring experiments to specific learning goals.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.4 Example Experiments
Here are some common experiments you can perform with phyphox:

Simple Pendulum: Using the accelerometer, measure period and damping.
Free Fall: Drop the phone safely and verify acceleration due to gravity.
Roller Coaster Analysis: Record acceleration and forces experienced during rides.
Sound Frequency Analysis: Capture and analyze sound waves and resonance frequencies.
Magnetic Field Mapping: Map spatial variations in magnetic fields using the magnetometer.
Barometric Altitude: Track altitude changes when climbing stairs or hills.
Rotational Dynamics: Study spinning motions and angular velocities.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.5 Applications in Education
phyphox fits perfectly into physics education at many levels:

Hands-On Learning: Students perform real experiments rather than only simulations or theory.
Inquiry-Based Teaching: Encourages hypothesis, measurement, data analysis, and interpretation.
Cost-Effective Labs: Removes the need for expensive dedicated sensors.
Remote or Hybrid Learning: Supports experimentation outside of traditional classrooms.
Cross-Disciplinary Connections: Links physics to technology, engineering, and data science.

Teachers can integrate phyphox into their lesson plans easily. For example, when teaching kinematics, students can measure acceleration during a walk or in a car; when discussing waves, they can analyze sound frequencies or light intensities.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:

Supported Platforms: Android (Google Play Store) and iOS (Apple App Store).
Device Requirements: Modern smartphones with the relevant sensors (most devices made in the last 5–7 years).
Cost: Free with no ads or in-app purchases.
Languages: Available in multiple languages, including English, German, Spanish, and more.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.1 Basic Theory
The size of a force is measured in units called Newtons (N). You can get a rough idea of a force’s size by thinking about the pull of the Earth on us.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.1.1 Mass
This is the amount of stuff (matter) in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) and is always the same wherever the object is. The only way to change the mass of something is to chip a bit off! (Ignoring relativistic effects of course.)


6.1.2 Weight
The force of attraction of the Earth on us is our WEIGHT. The more massive we are the bigger is the force of attraction and the bigger is our weight. This also gives us a rough definition of the Newton. A Newton is the pull of the Earth on about 100 g. The pull of the Earth on 1 kg is about 10 N.


6.1.3 Newton’s First Law (Law of Inertia)

An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force.
This means: \[
\text{If } \sum \vec{F} = 0, \quad \vec{v} = \text{constant}
\]



6.1.4 Newton’s Second Law (Law of Acceleration)

The acceleration \(\vec{a}\) of an object is proportional to the net force \(\sum \vec{F}\) acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass \(m\): \[
\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}
\]
This law quantifies how forces change motion.



6.1.5 Newton’s Third Law (Action-Reaction)

For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force: \[
\vec{F}_{\text{AB}} = - \vec{F}_{\text{BA}}
\]
Forces always come in pairs acting on two different objects.



6.1.6 Implications and Applications

Objects at rest or moving uniformly have zero net force.
To change motion, a force must be applied.
The same magnitude force applied to different masses results in different accelerations.
Reaction forces explain propulsion, walking, rocket thrust, etc.



6.1.7 Summary Table








Law
Statement
Formula




First Law
Object remains in uniform motion unless force acts
\(\sum \vec{F} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{v} = \text{constant}\)


Second Law
Force causes acceleration proportional to mass
\(\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}\)


Third Law
Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite
\(\vec{F}_{\text{AB}} = -\vec{F}_{\text{BA}}\)



To change the way an object is moving you need a force.
This force can either:

speed up the object, like a sprinter at the start of a race or..
slow down the object, like a motorbike slowing down as it approaches a red traffic signal or..
change the direction in which the object is moving, like a car turning a corner

Newton’s three laws of motion may be summarised as follows:

A body remains at rest or in a state of uniform motion unless acted on by a force. What is still stays still and what is moving stays moving at a steady speed in a straight line unless a force acts on it.
The resultant force on a body causes an acceleration which depends on both the size of the force and the mass of the body, i.e. \(\text{Force} = \text{Mass} \times  \text{Acceleration}\)
If a force acts on one body an equal and opposite force acts on another body.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.2 Stories to enrich

6.2.1 Newton’s Apple: A Story of Stillness and Insight
The famous apple story is actually true, at least according to the Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton’s Life, written by William Stukeley, an archaeologist and one of Newton’s first biographers. Stukeley records his conversation with Newton as follows:

“After dinner, the weather being warm, we went into the garden and drank tea, under the shade of some apple trees…he told me, he was just in the same situation, as when formerly, the notion of gravitation came into his mind. It was occasion’d by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood. Why should that apple always descend perpendicularly to the ground, thought he to himself…”

you can read the book, published in 1752 here:





Rather brilliantly, a piece of Newton’s apple tree was taken into space by British-born astronaut Piers Sellers as part of the 350 year celebrations.


6.2.2 The Horse and Cart Debate That Divided Philosophers
When Newton’s Third Law was proposed, critics raised a question: if a horse pulls on a cart, and the cart pulls back equally, how does anything move? This wasn’t just a joke—it sparked a genuine puzzle. The answer lies in the interaction with the ground: the horse pushes backward on the Earth, which pushes it forward. Newton’s Third Law is not a paradox, but a law of equal pairs, not cancellation. This insight became essential in understanding propulsion—whether walking, rowing, or spaceflight.
Reflection: How can a misunderstanding of Newton’s First and Third Law lead to confusion in everyday reasoning?


6.2.3 The Duel of Masks and the Vacuum Chamber
In 1654, Otto von Guericke, mayor of Magdeburg, staged a spectacle to demonstrate the force of air pressure and inertia. He created two large copper hemispheres, evacuated the air from within, and then hitched teams of horses to either side. Despite their efforts, the hemispheres could not be pulled apart. What amazed the public was not just the demonstration of pressure, but the indirect implication of Newton’s First Law: the air (or lack of it) was exerting a massive force, even though nothing visible was “pushing.”



The original Magdeburg hemispheres.




6.2.4 The Nuclear Cannon
One of the fastest moving man-made objects ever fired was not a specially designed projectile so much as a manhole cover. The 1957 Pascal-B nuclear test in Nevada was an underground nuclear detonation. The 900 kg steel plate that capped the well down to the explosive was blown off the top of a test shaft so rapidly that the high-speed camera footage of the incident captured the manhole cover in just one frame. Working from the framerate we conclude that the speed must have been more than 66 km/s. The plate was never found, and although the plate exceeded Earth’s escape velocity, it is most likely to have been vaporised by compression heating on it’s way through the atmosphere.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.3 Practical work and Demos

6.3.1 Newton’s 2nd Law experiment
The classic physics experiment is the N2 experiment in which a small trolley which is accelerated along a friction-compensated track by a number of small masses (washers are ideal) tied to a thread which is fixed to the trolley after passing over a pulley.The friction compensated track removes the effect of the work done against friction by the cart and is achieved by simply tilting the track until the cart, pushed lightly, continues to roll down the slope at steady speed.
We usually use lightgates to measure the acceleration by measuring the difference in velocity at two points a measured time interval apart. You can also directly measure acceleration with lightgates or accelerometers (phyphox is great for this).
If you don’t have any such technology available, or if you want to do it a bit differently you can time the trolley from a standing start over a known distance and then use: \[s = ut + 0.5 at^{2}\]
where:

\(t\) is the time period measured
\(u\) is the initial velocity (0)
\(a\) is the acceleration to be calculated
\(s\) is the measured distance

to calculate the average acceleration. Another variation with a speed only sensor would be to use: \[v^{2}=u^{2} + 2as\]
where:

\(v\) is the final velocity measured
\(u\) is the initial velocity (0)
\(a\) is the acceleration to be calculated
\(s\) is the measured distance

Despite being the experiment, an awful lot of students conduct it incorrectly. In order to get meaningful results it’s important to ensure mass being accelerated is constant. This means it’s critical to transfer the weights from the trolley to the accelerating mass or vice versa. In other words, when you plot graphs of acceleration against force The total mass of all objects accelerating is the constant gradient.
One of the odd issues with this experiment that you can get round with modern technology is that we take the accelerating force as mg - using the very law that we are trying to verify. If you have accelerometer and force meter available you can measure the quantities directly. Plotting the values against each other should validate N2 although if you have a very able class you could use an elastic attachment from the force meter to the car and have some fun…

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.4 1st law & 3rd law pairs.
A common misconception arises when people confuse Newton’s First Law with the action-reaction pairs described in Newton’s Third Law. Newton’s First Law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force, emphasizing how motion changes only when forces are unbalanced. In contrast, Newton’s Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction — forces always come in pairs acting on different objects. The confusion often lies in thinking that these action-reaction forces cancel each other out and thus prevent motion, but this is incorrect because they act on separate bodies. For example, when you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you equally, but these forces act on different objects and do not cancel in the sense of preventing movement altogether; whether motion occurs depends on other forces acting on each object. Understanding that First Law forces sum on a single object while Third Law pairs act on different objects is key to resolving this confusion.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.5 Rockets
The propulsion systems of rockets depend on the laws of momentum conservation and are well explained by the three newtonian laws. For a solid or liquid fuel rocket, the greater the velocity of the exhaust gases the greater is their momentum and hence the greater the momentum of the rocket.
When fuel burns in the rocket’s combustion chamber it creates hot, high-pressure gas made of billions of fast-moving particles. These particles zoom around randomly and collide with the chamber walls in all directions.Particles hit all the walls equally (left, right, top, bottom). Were these forces to balance, as they do perpendicular to the rocket, there’d be no resultant force/
At the nozzle opening however, the gas particles escape out the nozzle at high speed. This means that there’s fewer collisions on the nozzle side’s wall compared to the front wall. This imbalance of pressure inside the chamber creates a net force pushing the rocket forward.

6.5.1 Calculating Rocket Velocity with Changing Mass, Gravity, and Air Resistance
Calculating the velocity of a rocket properly is mathematically demanding - Let’s take a very crude model as an example:

Changing mass
Gravity
Air resistance (drag)


1. Ideal Rocket Equation (No Air Resistance)
In space (no gravity, no air), we start with the Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation:
\[
\Delta v = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)
\]
where:

\(\Delta v\) = change in velocity

\(v_e\) = exhaust velocity of the gases

\(m_0\) = initial mass (rocket + fuel)

\(m_f\) = final mass (after fuel burned)



2. Including Gravity
If launching vertically near Earth, gravity subtracts velocity, note that this assumes that we dont stray far enough to consider Earth’s gravitational field as anything other than uniform:
\[
v(t) = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m(t)}\right) - g \, t
\]
where \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity (≈ 9.81 m/s²).


3. Air Resistance (Drag)
Drag force is given by:
\[
F_{\text{drag}} = \frac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A
\]
where:

\(\rho\) = air density

\(v\) = rocket velocity

\(C_D\) = drag coefficient (shape-dependent)

\(A\) = cross-sectional area

Drag reduces the rocket’s net acceleration:
\[
a = \frac{T - F_{\text{drag}} - m \, g}{m}
\]
where:

\(T\) = thrust force

\(m\) = rocket mass at time \(t\)

Since \(m\) changes as fuel burns, we get a differential equation:
\[
m(t) \, \frac{dv}{dt}
=
T
-
\frac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A
-
m(t) \, g
\]


4. Full Differential Equation
We can express the velocity change as:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{dv}{dt}
=
\frac{T}{m(t)}
-
\frac{1}{2} \frac{\rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A}{m(t)}
-
g
}
\]
and:
\[
m(t) = m_0 - \dot{m} \cdot t
\]
where \(\dot{m}\) is the mass flow rate (fuel used per second).
Because drag depends on \(v\), and \(\rho\) changes with altitude, we usually solve this numerically.

title: 19  Gravity
text:
19.1.1 Gravitational Force
Newton’s law of universal gravitation: \[
F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}
\] Where: - \(F\) = gravitational force between two masses (N) - \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2\text{/kg}^2\) (gravitational constant) - \(m_1, m_2\) = masses (kg) - \(r\) = distance between centers of masses (m)


19.1.2 Gravitational Field Strength (\(g\))

Defined as force per unit mass: \[
g = \frac{F}{m}
\]
Near Earth’s surface, approximately: \[
g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2
\]
Direction of \(g\) is towards the mass creating the field.



19.1.3 Gravitational Field Due to a Point Mass
\[
g = \frac{GM}{r^2}
\] Where: - \(M\) = mass creating the field (kg) - \(r\) = distance from the mass center (m)


19.1.4 Gravitational Potential (\(\phi\))

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass to bring a small test mass from infinity to that point: \[
\phi = -\frac{GM}{r}
\]
Negative sign indicates work done by the field.



19.1.5 Relationship Between \(g\) and \(\phi\)
\[
g = -\frac{d\phi}{dr}
\]
Gravitational field strength is the spatial rate of change of gravitational potential.


19.1.6 Potential Energy in a Gravitational Field

Gravitational potential energy of a mass \(m\) at distance \(r\): \[
U = m\phi = - \frac{GMm}{r}
\]



19.1.7 Escape Velocity

The minimum velocity needed to escape the gravitational field without further propulsion: \[
v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}
\] Where:
\(R\) = radius of the planet/star (m)



19.1.8 Orbits and Circular Motion

For a satellite orbiting mass \(M\) at radius \(r\), centripetal force provided by gravity: \[
\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{GMm}{r^2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}
\]
Orbital period \(T\): \[
T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi r^{3/2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{GM}}
\]



19.1.9 Uniform Gravitational Field Approximation

Near Earth’s surface, \(g\) is nearly constant over small distances.
Use \(F = mg\) for weight and \(W = mgh\) for gravitational potential energy changes.

When an object falls from rest and accelerates under the effect of the Earth’s gravity the distance it falls (h) in a time t is given by the equation: \(h =  (gt^{2})\). The gravitational field strength at the surface of the Earth is approximately \(9.81 \text{Nkg}^{-1}\) and this will give a mass of one kg an acceleration of $9.81 ^{-1} $. That means that if an object is dropped near the Earth’s surface its speed increases by about \(10 \text{ms}^{-1}\) every second if the effects of air resistance are ignored.
When a projectile is thrown it has a constant vertical acceleration (g) towards the ground but a constant horizontal velocity if we ignore air resistance. The horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
In some of the experiments a constant head apparatus is mentioned. This is simply a device for maintaining a constant head of water at an outlet.

title: 19  Gravity
text:
19.2 Stories to enritch

19.2.1 Newton’s Apple and the Invisible Pull
The famous story of Isaac Newton watching an apple fall is more than legend. Newton realized that the same invisible force pulling the apple to Earth also kept the Moon orbiting. He imagined Earth’s gravity extending outward — a gravitational field acting at a distance. This idea was revolutionary: forces no longer needed to touch objects to act on them.
Reflection: How did imagining an invisible field change the way we understand forces?


19.2.2 Cavendish’s “Weighing the Earth” Experiment
In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the incredibly tiny gravitational attraction between two lead spheres using a torsion balance. From this, he calculated the gravitational constant (G) and estimated Earth’s mass. His delicate experiment was the first to measure gravity as a force between masses directly and gave birth to quantitative gravitational fields.
Reflection: How can measuring tiny forces help us understand huge planets?


19.2.3 Einstein’s Elevator: Gravity as Curved Space
Albert Einstein’s “thought experiment” of an elevator falling freely led to a radical insight: gravity isn’t just a force pulling objects, but a curvature of spacetime itself—a gravitational field as geometry. This shifted physics from Newton’s “force at a distance” to Einstein’s general relativity, fundamentally changing how we see gravity.
Reflection: What does it mean to say gravity is geometry, not just force?


19.2.4 The Mystery of Mercury’s Orbit
By the late 1800s, astronomers noticed Mercury’s orbit shifted slightly each orbit—a problem Newtonian gravity couldn’t explain fully. Einstein’s gravitational field equations later accounted for this “perihelion precession,” providing one of the first major tests of general relativity.
Reflection: How can tiny orbital quirks reveal deep truths about gravity?


19.2.5 The First Gravitational Wave Detection
In 2015, the LIGO observatory measured ripples in spacetime caused by colliding black holes—direct evidence of dynamic gravitational fields moving at light speed. This discovery confirmed Einstein’s prediction and opened a new way to “hear” the universe’s most violent events.
Reflection: How is gravity more than just a static pull? How can it ripple?


19.2.6 The Falling Feather and the Feather and the Hammer on the Moon
Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a feather and a hammer on the Moon’s surface. Without air resistance, both hit the ground at the same time—showing gravity’s uniform effect on all masses. This simple demonstration revealed the universality of free fall—a key idea in gravitational fields.
Reflection: Why do objects fall the same way regardless of their mass?


19.2.7 Black Holes: Gravity’s Ultimate Prison
Black holes form when gravity’s field becomes so intense that not even light can escape. Scientists realized these objects challenge classical ideas about gravitational fields, warping spacetime into regions with event horizons. Studying black holes pushes the limits of our understanding of gravity.
Reflection: What does it mean for gravity to be so strong it traps light?


19.2.8 Galileo’s Tower of Pisa Experiment (Maybe)
Legend says Galileo dropped balls of different masses from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, showing they fall at the same rate, disproving Aristotle’s idea that heavier objects fall faster. This was an early insight into gravitational acceleration and helped lay the groundwork for gravitational fields.
Reflection: How did questioning ancient beliefs lead to new physics?


19.2.9 The Earth-Moon Dance: Tides and Fields
Tides arise because the Moon’s gravitational field pulls harder on the near side of Earth than the far side, creating bulges in the oceans. This subtle effect of gravitational fields governs coastal life and ocean currents. It’s a beautiful example of how gravity shapes life on Earth.
Reflection: How does gravity reach across space to move oceans?


19.2.10 The Pioneer Anomaly: Gravity’s Unexplained Pull?
In the late 20th century, the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft showed tiny unexplained deviations from predicted trajectories. Scientists wondered if our understanding of gravitational fields was incomplete. Though later explained by heat recoil forces, the mystery inspired new investigations into gravity’s reach.
Reflection: What can small anomalies teach us about big forces?

Age range: 16-18 Apparatus required: o Two power balls •Piece of elastic

9. Falling can and water - what happens?

Take a tin can and drill a hole in the bottom. The size isn’t critical but two or three millimetres in diameter will be fine. Put your finger over the hole and fill the can with water. Now drop the can - the water stays inside.
This is much as you would expect, since all objects accelerate downwards at the same rate if air resistance is ignored. Now repeat the experiment but drop the can after you have allowed some of the water to start streaming out. What happens to the water? It looks as if the can is continuing to empty itself, but this would mean that the water is falling with a greater acceleration than g.
This is impossible of course! The can and the water both accelerate at the same rate, g, and the can has the same amount of water in it when it reaches the ground as it had at the start of the drop.

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Bowl or bucket •Tin can with hole



19.3.15 The contracting stream
The speed of a jet of water falling vertically from a tap into a sink increases the further from the tap it gets. This would seem to suggest that more water reaches the sink every second than is being emitted from the tap. Clearly impossible! This can only be explained if the stream of water gets thinner with increasing depth below the tap. This can be verified by turning the tap on slightly and observing the stream.

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: ’Water tap



19.3.16 Falling slinky
A variation of experiment nine is to drop an extended helical spring and observe what happens to various parts of it as it falls. You will find that during the drop the bottom coils stay where they are while the upper coils catch up with them and then the whole spring falls together. During the whole motion the centre of mass falls with an acceleration of g. The information that the spring is falling will take a certain time to travel down the spring and so initially the bottom part of the spring “thinks” it is still being held up and so remains at rest. (Thanks to Martin for this idea)
Using a TV camera to record the fall and looking at a slow motion replay will make the results of many experiments much easier to appreciate.

19.3.17 Monkey and hunter
A monkey hangs from a tree in a jungle and is discovered by a hunter who decides to shoot it. Pointing the rifle between the eyes of the monkey he prepares to pull the trigger. The monkey, being fairly intelligent, reasons that if he waits until the moment the bullet leaves the barrel and then drops out of the tree the bullet will pass over his head. The hunter pulls the trigger, the monkey waits until the bullet is leaving the barrel and then lets go. To his dismay the bullet hits him directly between the eyes! He was intelligent but had forgotten his Physics!
The explanation for this can be demonstrated by a classic experiment that shows the constancy of acceleration for falling bodies.
Mount an electromagnet in a clamp about 0.5 m above the bench and mount a blowpipe horizontally in another clamp so that it is pointing just below the core of the electromagnet. Put a marble in the blowpipe, fix a small strip of aluminium foil across the mouth of the blowpipe and then connect up a series circuit with the electromagnet, a d.c. power source and the aluminium strip.
Switch on and hang a tin lid from the electromagnet making sure that the blowpipe is pointing at the centre of the tin. Blow sharply down the pipe and the marble will fly out, breaking the foil, and causing the tin lid to fall. The marble will fall at the same rate as the tin lid and should collide with it before hitting the bench.

19.3.18 Dropping books and paper - air resistance and drag
This is an interesting experiment on air friction, but it is important to stop between each part and ask the students what happens next?

Drop a sheet of paper - it falls slowly due to air friction
Now crumple it up - its mass is unaltered but the crumpling reduces the air friction and so it falls quicker
Then use another, similar flat sheet of paper, but this time with a book on top of it; the effect of the air friction on the paper is removed
Then a sheet of paper with a book underneath it - they both fall together (e) And finally a ream of loose paper - all the sheets fall at the same rate.

An alternative to parts (c) and (d) is to use a metal disc with a similar sized paper disc placed either on top of it or below it.
These experiments remove the need for the traditional guinea and feather experiment if you don’t have a vacuum pump.
Extension experiments:

Make paper versions of helicopter blades, and investigate their motion when dropped
Investigate the motion of simple parachutes made in the form of paper cones! > 7-18 > > •A stack of loose paper •A book of similar area •Scissors >



19.3.19 Galileo inclined planes
An interesting effect of the acceleration along inclined planes can be shown by a variation of Galileo’s experiment on diluted gravity. Thread a bead onto each of a set of wires starting at one point on a vertical bicycle wheel from which the spokes have been removed and ending at different points along the circumference. When the beads are released from the top they slide down the wires keeping a circular arrangement and all reaching the end of the chord at the same time.


19.3.20 Falling through the Earth
A related problem in gravitation refers to the fact that it takes 42 minutes for objects falling through holes in the Earth to reach the other side whatever chord is used. (This is of course a theoretical and ideal situation and ignores all frictional effects!) It would make an ideal and rapid transport system. You can extend the idea to SHM where the body is free to oscillate about the centre of the Earth. Students often find it difficult to accept that the acceleration is zero at the centre of the “fall”.


19.3.21 Guinea and feather tube
This is a classic experiment to show the effect of air resistance and the constancy of the acceleration due to gravity. Take a 1 m long glass tube of diameter about 5 cm, put a small piece of feather and a penny into the tube and fit bungs tightly into both ends - one with a metal tube in the centre. Attach the tube to a vacuum pump. Upend the tube and show that the penny falls faster than the feather because it has much lower air resistance. Now pump out the air and show that they both fall at the same rate.
A video clip of astronauts dropping a falcon feather and a hammer on the Moon illustrates this as well. (It is important to realise that on the Moon there is no air, but there is still a gravitational field, about 1/6 of that at the surface of the Earth.) It is certainly not true to say that no air means no gravity.

19.3.22 Falling can with hole at one side
The can with holes (see liquid pressure) can be used to demonstrate that if there is no gravitational attraction there will be no liquid pressure. For this experiment use a can with just one hole in one side near the bottom. Fill it with water, cover the hole with your finger and then drop it. Since both can and water fall together there is no net gravitational force and so the water stays in the can.

Theory:
Pressure at a point in a liquid = hpg, and since the net value of g is zero for the falling can and water there is no pressure difference between the top and bottom of the water in the can.
Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: ’Tin can with hole near the bottom •Water



19.3.23 A floating block in a falling jar
A jar about half full of water has a block of wood (or loaded straw) floating in the water and is suspended from a helical spring. Initially the jar is supported. If the jar is released, the water level stays at the same place in the jar and the block floats at the same level as it falls.

Theory:
The depth at which the block floats depends on its weight and the upthrust on it. The upthrust depends on the weight of water displaced, and so, as the acceleration of the jar and block change, BOTH the weight of the block and the upthrust change in the same way — the block floats at the same depth as it falls.
Objects in accelerated frames of reference behave in the same way as they would in gravitational fields. The falling on the spring is subject to a varying acceleration just like it would be if it were taken to the Moon where the gravitational acceleration is less. This is a very useful demonstration of one of the ideas of General Relativity! (Thanks to MartiN for this idea)
Age range: 11-18 depending on the treatment of the theory Apparatus required: •Jar •Water •Wooden block •Helical spring



19.3.24 Two tennis balls.
Take two tennis balls and inject one with water. (Make sure that it is completely full.) The balls
Then ask them to hold the balls to show that although they are of different mass they still accelerate at the same rate in a gravitational field.

(N.B The injected ball will re-seal itself when the needle is withdrawn)

19.3.25 Smiley pop ups and projectile motion
In his book ‘Experiments in Physics’ Colin Siddons ( * ) suggested using these small ‘pop-up’ toys to study projectile motion. This is a really good idea and can form the basis of an investigation for students aged 14-18. The toys, called Smiley Pop UPS, are very cheap and introduce a bit of fun into the experiment.
You squash the toy on to the bench and then, as the rubber sucker slowly comes off, the toy launches itself into the air. Since the same spring is used each time the launching force should be the same. This means that both vertical motion and motion at an angle to the vertical can be investigated. For the angled motion use tilted runways or even tilt the lab tables where this is possible. Fixing a pin through a piece of sellotape stuck to the ramp or putting a piece of rough paper on the slope will stop the toys slipping down the slope.
Theory:

The range of an object projected at an angle A to the horizontal can be found as follows. The object will hit the ground again when h = O, i.e. when ut sin A = h gt2 Therefore it will hit the ground after a time t, where t = 2u sin A/g.
Therefore the range R is given by:
R = horizontal velocity x time = [ucos Ax 2u sin A]/g = [u 2 sin A cos A]/g = u2sin 2A/g
This range is of course the horizontal range from the point of launch.
Age range: 14-19
Apparatus required: •Smiley pop up (or similar) •Ruler •Ramp •Rough paper or pin •Sellotape

title: 24  NuclearPhysics
text:
24.1.1 Nuclear Notation
A nucleus is represented as: \[
{}^A_Z\text{X}
\] Where: - \(A\) = mass number (number of nucleons = protons + neutrons) - \(Z\) = atomic number (number of protons) - \(\text{X}\) = chemical symbol
Neutron number: \(N = A - Z\)


24.1.2 Nuclear Forces

Strong nuclear force holds nucleons together:

Attractive at ~1–3 fm

Repulsive below ~0.5 fm (to prevent collapse)


Overcomes electrostatic repulsion between protons



24.1.3 Mass-Energy Equivalence
Einstein’s equation: \[
E = mc^2
\] Where: - \(E\) = energy (J) - \(m\) = mass (kg) - \(c\) = speed of light (\(3.0 \times 10^8\) m/s)


24.1.4 Mass Defect and Binding Energy
Mass defect: Difference between the mass of separated nucleons and the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy: Energy required to break a nucleus into its constituent nucleons.
\[
E_b = \Delta m \cdot c^2
\]
Binding energy per nucleon = \(\frac{E_b}{A}\)

Indicates stability of nucleus
Peaks at iron (\({}^{56}\text{Fe}\))



24.1.5 Radioactive Decay

Types:

Alpha (\(\alpha\)): Helium nucleus \({}^4_2\text{He}\)
Beta-minus (\(\beta^-\)): Neutron \(\rightarrow\) proton + electron + antineutrino
Beta-plus (\(\beta^+\)): Proton \(\rightarrow\) neutron + positron + neutrino
Gamma (\(\gamma\)): High-energy photon; often emitted after \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) decay



Example equations:
Alpha: \[
{}^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^4_2\text{He}
\]
Beta-minus: \[
{}^{14}_6\text{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_7\text{N} + \beta^- + \bar{\nu}_e
\]
Beta-plus: \[
{}^{11}_6\text{C} \rightarrow {}^{11}_5\text{B} + \beta^+ + \nu_e
\]



24.1.6 Exponential Decay
Number of undecayed nuclei: \[
N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}
\]
Activity: \[
A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}
\]
Decay constant and half-life: \[
T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
\]


24.1.7 Nuclear Reactions

Fission: Heavy nucleus splits into smaller ones, releasing energy
Fusion: Light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy

Example (fusion in stars): \[
{}^2_1\text{H} + {}^3_1\text{H} \rightarrow {}^4_2\text{He} + n + \text{energy}
\]
Fission example (uranium-235): \[
{}^{235}_{92}\text{U} + n \rightarrow {}^{144}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{89}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3n + \text{energy}
\]


24.1.8 Binding Energy Curve

Graph of binding energy per nucleon vs. mass number
Explains why:

Fusion releases energy for \(A < 56\)
Fission releases energy for \(A > 56\)




24.1.9 Detecting Radiation

Geiger-Müller tube
Cloud chamber
Photographic film
Background radiation must be accounted for



24.1.10 Applications of Nuclear Physics

Medical: PET scans, cancer radiotherapy
Energy: Nuclear reactors (fission), fusion research
Dating: Carbon-14 dating
Industrial: Tracers, thickness gauges



24.1.11 Safety and Shielding

Ionising radiation damages tissue and DNA
Safety measures:

Limit time exposed
Increase distance
Use shielding (e.g. lead, concrete)




24.1.12 1. Simple atom analogy/model
A simple way of remembering the relative sizes of the nucleus and the atom of hydrogen is to imagine that if the nucleus is represented by a ball 1 cm in diameter (say a marble) the orbiting electron would be 1 km away.
The ratio of the diameter of the atom to that of the nucleus is about 1 to 100 000.

Theory
The radius of a nucleus is given by the equation:
r = roAl/3 where A is the nucleon number of the nucleus and ro is a constant (1.3x10 15 m)



24.1.13 2. Alpha particle scattering - two alternatives
There are two simple alternatives to the commercially available “tin hat” apparatus to demonstrate alpha particle scattering by a nucleus.

Fix a rubber sucker to a glass sheet placed on an overhead projector. Now roll a ball bearing towards it. The disadvantage of this method is the relatively small size of the sucker.
Use a fixed circular magnet representing the nucleus, and then swing another small magnet towards it to represent the alpha particle (In this version it is important to keep a repulsion between the two magnets by using a suitable method of suspension.)


Age range: 14-18 Apparatus required: •Overhead projector •Ball bearings •Rubber sucker •Magnets



24.1.14 3. Rutherford scattering - a permanent record
A permanent record of the Rutherford scattering experiments can be obtained by using the tin hat simulation of the field but putting it on a piece of white paper resting on carbon paper. Draw a set of lines on the white paper to show the direction of incident ball bearings. Roll the ball bearings down a ramp, and the pressure on the carbon paper will give a permanent record of their tracks after “collision” with the “nucleus”. (The ball bearings can be collected by surrounding the apparatus by a magnetic strip or simply just catching them!)

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Tin hat apparatus •Ball bearings •White paper •Carbon paper •Flexible magnetic strip (optional)
Nuclear



24.1.15 4. Rutherford scattering
Use a row of pins hidden inside a box to represent the nuclei of a set of atoms. Roll ball bearings into the box through a hole in one side, and observe where they come out. Get pupils to predict what sort of obstacles are in the box.


24.1.16 5. Plum pudding model
If we are going to use the special metal tin hat model to simulate the nuclear model of an atom, then we should show the alternative plum pudding simulation. Instead of the “tin hat” I have used a cymbal - the ball bearing will roll across the centre quite easily, showing reduced scattering by this type of atom. There is a deflection, but if the ball bearings are rolled from about half way up the little ramp no ball bearing ever suffers more than a 90 0 deflection.

Theory
The much lower electric field intensity of the plum pudding model is represented by the lower central height of the cymbal. The potential at the centre is also much smaller resulting in a smaller deflection by the incident alpha particles.

Age range: 16-18 Apparatus required: •Cymbal •Ball bearings


24.1.17 Mouse traps and chain reactions

This lovely (although potentially painful) demonstration is a splendid simulation of a nuclear chain reaction. Set up a number of cocked mouse traps side by side in a rectangle (a dozen will work well) to represent uranium nuclei. Put a couple of polystyrene balls representing neutrons on each one.

Throw in another polystyrene ball (neutron) to start the chain reaction. One mouse trap goes off - this sets off others and so on! A simulated chain reaction results.
The balls are shot all over the lab (fast neutrons). Spacing out the mouse traps gives an idea of the shape of fuel rods and the way a chain reaction can fail.
It works best if the mouse traps are placed on the lid of a cardboard box to give a good Ulinkage” between one “fission” and another.

Alternative methods are to use a set of matches fixed upright in a block of wood - when you light one the others are set alight as the flame spreads through them like a forest fire. You could also knock down a set of dominoes by touching the first one and making it fall so that it collides with another and so on.


Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Mouse traps •Polystyrene balls •Block of wood with holes •Matches •Dominoes •Cardboard box

Nuclear


24.1.18 7. E20 note and ball - nuclear forces
These two analogies are designed to explain the forces between sub-nuclear particles

A simulation of long-range electrostatic repulsive forces can be given by two people throwing a ball to each other, each one standing on a skateboard or wheeled trolley. The thrower recoils when they throw the ball, and the catcher recoils when they receive it. There is no limit to the range of the force as long as they throw hard enough.
The short-range strong nuclear force (only effective over distances less than about 10 15 m) can be represented by the two people trying to throw a E20 note to each other. For a start there is no possibility of them throwing it to each other unless they are close together because of the large amount of air resistance; it will only work at short distances, but it is certainly attractive!


Theory
Both these experiments are simulations of the exchange of force carriers when a force acts between two objects - a photon in the case of the electromagnetic force and a gluon in the case of the strong nuclear force.
Ensure that a clear space is available. Control the ball throwing. Only pupils who know how to use a skate board should take part in experiment (a).

Age range: 16-18 Apparatus required: o Two heavy balls •Two skateboards •Two notes


24.1.19 8. Nuclear fusion analogy!
The problem of the repulsion between two nuclei and the existence of a short-range nuclear force can be explained as follows.
Imagine two people wearing large inflatable suits so that each appears to be standing in the centre of a balloon. The suits are so large that if they stand near each other they cannot hold hands. Only by the people running together at high speed will the suits be sufficiently squashed for them to be able to grasp each other’s hand and so “fuse”!


24.1.20 9. Strong nuclear force — attraction and a boomerang
To demonstrate the attractive nature of a force due to the interchange of virtual particles between protons, think of two people standing fairly close together on skateboards but facing away from each other. One throws a boomerang to the other. The boomerang curves round and is caught by the second person, so pushing the two people together.


24.1.21 10. Nuclear collisions - watches
To discover the composition of subatomic particles two particles are fired towards each other at high speed. An example of this is the Large Electron Positron Collider (LEP) at CERN in Geneva where electrons and positrons are made to collide head on in the giant accelerator. In a way this is rather a crude method. It is a bit like trying to find out what is in a watch by throwing two watches together and seeing what bits fly out. The big difference between the analogy and the subatomic particles is that in the nuclear collisions some bits that fly out were not there before the collision; they have been “made” by the conversion of energy to matter in the collision - certainly not true with the watches!

Nuclear


11. Accelerator models
Here are two ideas to simulate the action of a particle accelerator where the particle gets a kick every time it passes between two accelerating electrodes, the first a synchrotron (constant radius) and the second a cyclotron.

Make a large circular orbit out of plastic curtain rail. Put a marble inside the ring touching the wall to represent the particle, and use an air blower to simulate the kick given by the electric field as the particle orbits the accelerator. If a small section of the track could be made to open, you can simulate the extraction of a charged particle from an accelerator by a magnetic field. A ball fixed to a thread might do as well - no accelerator walls. This simulates the operation of a synchrotron where the orbit radius is fixed and the confining magnetic field is made to increase as the particle’s energy increases.
In the second method all you need is a ball suspended by a string from a post (sometimes used to train young children to play tennis) and a bat. Give the ball a push, so that it swings round the post, and every time it passes you give it a hit with the bat. The ball will gain energy on each orbit, move faster and so swing out further from the post.

This simulates the operation of a cyclotron where the magnetic field is constant and the orbit radius increases as the particle’s energy increases.
Adding a horizontal string, fixed between the ball and the vertical central post, to the swing ball simulates synchrotron operation. As the ball is hit, its velocity increases, but the horizontal string prevents it from changing its orbit radius. However, as its gets faster the centripetal force in the string increases — analogous to the increase in magnetic field in a synchrotron required to keep the particles in a constant orbit as they accelerate.

Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required:


•Length of plastic curtain rail (at least 2m) •Air blower •Polystyrene balls or marbles
•Ball on string tied to the top of a fixed post •Extra string •Bat

Nuclear


12. The bubble chamber
This simple experiment is an excellent demonstration of how a bubble chamber works and can also be used to reinforce the idea of a cloud chamber. Pour out a gassy drink such as lemonade, and allow it to stand for a few minutes until no more bubbles rise. Then drop in a small amount of fine salt (or sand). This gives nuclei for bubbles to form on, and you will see clouds of bubbles begin to rise through the liquid. In a similar manner ions are formed in a bubble chamber when a radioactive particle passes through, and bubbles form on these. Bubble chambers are more effective than cloud chambers, as there are more atoms that can be ionised and hence more “nuclei” on which bubbles can form.

Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Can of fizzy drink •Glass beaker •Salt




24.1.22 13. The power of the Sun
The power of the Sun can be found by measuring the amount of energy falling on a small area of the Earth’s surface every second.
Use a blackened tin can containing a known mass of water. Shield the can from the sunlight, measure its temperature, and then put it out in the sun for a known length of time and measure the final temperature. The energy gained by the water can be calculated, and knowing the area exposed to the sunlight enables you to find the energy falling on a square metre of the Earth’s surface per second — this is known as the solar constant. From this you can calculate the power of the Sun (see below).

Theory:
Take the solar constant to be 1370 Wm- at a distance equal to the radius (R) of the Earth’s orbit. This means that a total amount of energy equal to 4TtR2 x1370 J is passing out from the Sun every second.
Now the radius of the Earth’s orbit is 1.5x10 11 m and so the energy emitted by the Sun every second is:

E = x1370 = J.

Using Einstein’s mass-energy equation (E = mc ) you can calculate the mass of the Sun being converted into energy every second.
Mass converted to energy = E/c2

= 3.87x1026/9x1016 = kg
= 4.3x106 tonnes. Diagram not to scale

This means that the Sun is converting over four million tonnes of its mass into energy every second!
Age range: 16-18 Apparatus required: •Blackened tin can •Ruler •Thermometer •Stopclock or watch

25.1.1 Wave-Particle Duality

Light exhibits both wave and particle properties:

Wave: interference, diffraction
Particle: photoelectric effect

Matter (like electrons) also shows wave-like behaviour (e.g., electron diffraction).

de Broglie wavelength: \[
\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}
\] Where: - \(\lambda\) = wavelength (m) - \(h\) = Planck’s constant (\(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) Js) - \(p\) = momentum (kg·m/s)


25.1.2 The Photoelectric Effect

When light of sufficient frequency shines on a metal, electrons are emitted from its surface.

Einstein’s photoelectric equation: \[
hf = \phi + KE_{\text{max}}
\] Where: - \(h\) = Planck’s constant
- \(f\) = frequency of incident light
- \(\phi\) = work function (minimum energy needed to liberate an electron)
- \(KE_{\text{max}}\) = maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons
Threshold frequency: \[
f_{\text{min}} = \frac{\phi}{h}
\]


25.1.3 Evidence for Photons

No photoelectrons emitted below the threshold frequency, regardless of intensity.
Photoelectron emission is instantaneous if \(f > f_{\text{min}}\).
Increasing intensity increases number of photoelectrons, not their energy.
Only explained if light is made of quantised photons: \(E = hf\)



25.1.4 Energy Levels and Spectra

Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels.
Electrons absorb/emits quanta of energy to jump between levels: \[
\Delta E = hf
\]
Emission spectra: coloured lines on black background → electrons falling to lower levels.
Absorption spectra: dark lines on coloured background → electrons absorbing photons.



25.1.5 Electron Diffraction

Evidence that particles (e.g., electrons) behave as waves:

Electrons diffracted by thin graphite or crystal lattice
Shows interference patterns like light

Diffraction angle increases when:

Electron speed is lower (larger wavelength)
Crystal spacing is similar to wavelength

title: 25  Quanta
text:
25.2 Stories to enritch

25.2.1 Planck’s Quantum Leap
In 1900, Max Planck was trying to solve the puzzle of blackbody radiation—why heated objects emitted light with strange intensity patterns. He proposed that energy was emitted in discrete “quanta” rather than continuously. This radical idea launched quantum physics, overturning classical assumptions.
Reflection: How did imagining energy in packets change physics forever?


25.2.2 Einstein’s Photoelectric Puzzle
In 1905, Einstein explained how light could eject electrons from metals only if it had enough energy per “particle” (photon). This showed light behaves both as waves and particles, a cornerstone of quantum theory. His insight won the Nobel Prize and challenged the wave-only view of light.
Reflection: How can light be both a wave and a particle?


25.2.3 Schrödinger’s Cat: Alive, Dead, and Both
Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat sealed in a box with a quantum-triggered poison mechanism. According to quantum theory, until observed, the cat is in a superposition—both alive and dead simultaneously. This thought experiment highlighted the weirdness of quantum measurement.
Reflection: What does superposition mean for our everyday reality?


25.2.4 Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle: Limits of Knowing
Werner Heisenberg discovered there’s a fundamental limit to how precisely we can know both position and momentum of a particle at once. This uncertainty isn’t due to measurement flaws but a core property of nature. It changed how scientists think about reality and measurement.
Reflection: What does it mean that nature has built-in uncertainty?


25.2.5 The Double-Slit Experiment: Light’s Strange Behavior
When light (or electrons) pass through two slits, they create an interference pattern—like waves—yet behave like particles hitting the screen individually. This baffled physicists and revealed the dual nature of matter and light. It remains a central mystery and demonstration in quantum physics.
Reflection: How can particles create wave-like patterns?


25.2.6 Bohr’s Model and the Quantum Jump
Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit atoms only in certain fixed energy levels and “jump” between them by absorbing or emitting precise energy packets. This explained atomic spectra and introduced quantized energy states. His model was the first step toward modern quantum mechanics.
Reflection: Why do electrons only occupy certain energy levels?


25.2.7 The Quantum Revolution in Computing
In the late 20th century, scientists realized that quantum bits (qubits) could exist in superpositions, allowing quantum computers to process information in fundamentally new ways. This could revolutionize technology, breaking classical computational limits.
Reflection: How could quantum physics change computers forever?


25.2.8 The Strange World of Entanglement: Spooky Action at a Distance
Einstein called it “spooky action”—particles linked so that measuring one instantly determines the state of the other, no matter the distance. This entanglement defies classical ideas about locality and challenges our understanding of causality. Experiments confirm entanglement and drive quantum cryptography.
Reflection: What does entanglement say about the connectedness of the universe?


25.2.9 The Birth of Quantum Mechanics in a Café
Legend has it that in 1925, Werner Heisenberg worked in a small Danish café, formulating matrix mechanics—one of the earliest quantum theories—while scribbling on napkins. This humble setting birthed a mathematical framework explaining atomic behavior.
Reflection: How can a casual setting lead to revolutionary science?

25.3 Practical work and Demos

25.3.1 Flight of stairs and the quantum theory
One of the basic results of the quantum theory is that some energy states are not allowed. Because of the very small value of Planck’s constant (6.6x10 34 Js) we do not usually observe this discontinuity. However we could compare it to a flight of stairs down which a man and an ant are travelling. The steps are effectively classical to the man - he seems to travel down with an uninterrupted energy change - but they are of a quantum nature to the ant. It all depends on your scale of observation.


25.3.2 Quantum theory and milk
A man wants exactly a pint of milk. He can get it either by filling a bottle from a tap or by catching a carton as it comes off a conveyor belt. Filling the bottle from the tap represents the classical nature of Physics while using the discrete cartons represents the quantum idea. Notice that with the quantum analogy he may get a quantum (carton) immediately the belt is switched on or have to wait for some time for a carton to arrive. However when it does he will still get the whole carton at once. With the classical theory he gets milk as soon as the tap is turned on, but the rate of flow may be small, and he may not get a pint as quickly as he does by the quantum method!

Age range: 16-18



25.3.3 When the quantum theory becomes effective
This analogy attempts to show when the quantum theory would be observable in everyday life - a consequence of the value of Planck’s constant being very large, i.e. close to one. Imagine a soccer player trying to score a goal through a slot in a defensive wall. In normal life he would expect to be able to hit any part of the goal simply by changing his shooting position. However, if he finds that there are some places the ball cannot get to no matter where he stands, then thatl s when he has entered the realm of quantum soccer!
Quantum


25.3.4 Gamma radiation and the quantum theory
Revise the work done in earlier years on gamma radiation. Emphasise that it is part of the electromagnetic spectrum and therefore propagated as waves.
To show the quantum nature of this radiation use a gamma source and a Geiger counter connected to a loudspeaker via a ratemeter. Adjust the distance of the Geiger counter from the source so that the incident radiation is of low intensity. The students can hear the individual clicks as each photon arrives at the counter, showing the quantum nature of the radiation.

For details of the use of radioactive sources please see page 259.
Age range: 16-19
Apparatus required: •Gamma source •Geiger counter •Ratemeter •Loudspeaker •Leads



25.3.5 Quantum rainfall
Imagine that you are walking through a shower of rain. At the end of your walk you know that you will be wet. However, you do not get all the water at once! During the walk raindrops fall on you in a chaotic way, and you cannot predict when the next raindrop is going to hit you. The final result is that you are wet, but this is due to many raindrops.
These raindrops are analogous to the quanta in the quantum theory of radiation. The wetness represents the classical theory of radiation.

standing waves

vibration
generator


25.3.6 Electron waves in orbits
From Schrodinger’s wave equation we can imagine the electron as existing as a wave that fits round an orbit a given number of times.
In other words 21tr = nX where X is the electron wavelength, n is an integer and r is the radius of the orbit. A simulation of this idea is as follows. A ring of stiff wire should be fitted on top of a vibration generator - I use a loop about 15 - 20 cm in diameter. By adjusting the frequency of oscillation of the vibration generator, standing waves can be produced in the wire ring analogous to electron waves in the orbits of atoms. Multiple rings are impressive.
(b) An extension of this experiment shows the differing wavelengths further out from the nucleus. Two pieces of cord - one light and one heavy - are tied together. One end is fixed to a retort stand, and the other is attached to a vibration generator. When you switch on the generator, standing waves are produced in the cords. The frequency is the same in both, but the wavelength differs since the speed of the waves in the two cords is different.

Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Vibration generator o Loop of stiff wire •Signal generator •Retort stands •Pieces of cord



25.3.7 The quantum theory of radiation
Every time an electron falls from one energy level in an atom to another it emits a small ‘bundle’ of energy called a photon. The bigger the energy drop, the higher the frequency of the electromagnetic radiation.
The brightness of the source of light depends on the number of these photons emitted per second. The greater the number of photons, the brighter the light.
Each photon has a tiny energy and a 100 W lamp will emit roughly 100 million million million photons every second! Although they travel at the speed of light (300 000 km/s) they are so tiny that we don’t feel them hitting us. However, the radiation pressure from the impact of many millions upon millions of photons does have an effect on the tail of a comet, helping to keep it pointing away from the Sun.
